node.idea: With the pawn on g6 Black clears the way to fianchetto the bishop to g7, where it will rake the long diagonal from the corner straight through the centre toward White's queenside.
The bishop settles on g7 and immediately leans on the long diagonal; its first target is the knight on d4, the piece holding White's grip on the centre.

The bishop backs up the d4-knight and readies castling long — the sharp opposite-wings main line. Capturing on c6 instead would be a concession: Black recaptures toward the centre and the b-file opens against b2.

This is what keeps it an ACCELERATED Dragon: the knight comes to f6 before the d-pawn commits. Play the pawn to d6 now and White gets f3, transposing into a Main-Line Dragon; holding the pawn on its home square keeps the one-move central break in reserve.

A rule to burn in: once White's queen leaves its home square in a Dragon, look hard at the knight leap to g4. Trading that knight for the dark-squared bishop leaves the g7-bishop without a rival on its diagonal. The catch — after the leap the bishop can't step off e3, since the twice-attacked d4-knight would fall, so White's only try is to capture on c6 first.

With the concrete lines still murky, the soundest choice is to finish developing and castle. The pawn deliberately stays home: if White insists on a Main-Line Dragon setup, the central break in one move is the reward.

White castles long, and now the king and queen sit on the same file — that changes the whole assessment. The knight leap to g4 comes back on: after the capture on c6 and the bishop's move to d4, the bishop swings to h6 and pins the queen to the king. White blocks with f4, but then the e-pawn hits f4 and, with the pin freezing it, wins material.

The knight jumps in with a double point: it eyes the bishop on e3 and, with the queen no longer home, the whole h6-pin idea is live. The bishop still can't move — the d4-knight is attacked twice and would drop.

Recapturing toward the centre swings the b-file wide open, and with White castled long that file points straight at b2 — the attack writes itself. The c-pawn now becomes a battering ram against White's king cover.
There it is — the bishop swings to h6 and pins the queen to the king along the dark diagonal. The queen is nailed in place.

The crusher. The e-pawn strikes f4, and because the queen is pinned the pawn cannot capture back — it is as if f4 were not there — so the bishop on d4 falls and Black emerges a full piece up. Precision first, though: snatching with the bishop on f4 with check is the tempting error; after the king steps aside, taking on d4 lets White recapture and the f4-bishop is left hanging. Take on d4 first — the f4-pawn is not going anywhere.

This is the sting of the mainline: Black is often forced to push the pawn to e5, and the bishop drops to c5, shutting down the g7-bishop's diagonal. It takes much of the fun out of the Dragon, and White is considered better here.

The pawn to g5 chases the bishop off the board's active diagonal altogether. Booting the strong piece unburdens the position and lets Black consolidate the extra material in peace.

The knight to g4 with check is crushing — it drives the exposed king onto the run into a mating net, and Black's attack, a pawn up already, simply finishes the game.

node.idea: The pawn on c4 hands the knight a potential outpost on d4 — but there is no rush to sit on it. The knight comes to c6 first; the d4-hole is a long-term weakness that will tell only once everything is developed.
The fianchetto goes in. It concedes one thing — White can answer with the pawn to d4 and steer into a standard Maróczy Bind — but in return the g7-bishop gets a magnificent long diagonal.

With the bishop on g7 Black is already comfortably better: the dark squares in the centre are dominated, and White's light-squared bishop is stuck behind its own c4-, d3- and e4-pawns — a big pawn, not a piece.
The pawn to d6 improves the position and, more to the point, prepares to trade off the f3-knight with the bishop to g4 — the knight is White's main guard of the d4 square. The g8-knight can wait.
The bishop steps to g4, clamping down on d4 by threatening to trade the very piece that controls it. This is classic positional chess — remove the defender of the square you want.

Eliminate the knight while the chance is there. Trading the light-squared bishops is only fine for Black, but removing White's f3-knight — the guard of d4 — is the real prize, so take it now before it can slip away.
The Botvinnik setup: fianchetto plus the pawn to e6, carving out e7 as the developing square for the g8-knight. The pawns stand like teeth, gripping the central light squares White can never occupy.
The unassuming pawn to a6 is the first step of the real plan: preparing the b5 break to prise open the queenside where Black is stronger.
Now — and only now — the knight lands on d4, chosen at the most opportune moment rather than the first. It cements the grip while the queenside break is readied.
The knight to f3 with check is the clean finish — a fork that ends it at once, far quicker than grinding a simplified endgame a queen up.

node.idea: The Alekhine: Black offers the knight as a target, daring White's pawns forward. The whole opening is a provocation — let the centre advance, then strike at it.

This is the critical fork in the road. Three or four sound setups exist here; the Four Pawns Attack is the one for the player who wants to punish the Alekhine — little theory to learn, and a real chance to blow Black off the board.

The pawn to f4 completes the Four Pawns Attack — pawns on c4, d4, e4 and f4, absolute central domination. It is the most ambitious try, but it comes at the cost of development: play it carelessly and White can be crushed inside five moves.

Recapture toward the centre with the f-pawn — NOT with the d-pawn, which would invite an unfavourable queen trade. The plus of the whole system is a monster centre; the minus is lagging development, so precision is required.

The knight to c6 is the main line — and here is the pitfall: the natural knight to f3 is a mistake. It walks straight into the capture on d4 followed by the bishop pin on g4, dropping the e5-pawn. Nor does the knight to e2 help — it blocks the bishop.

The key restraint: do NOT push c5 to gain a tempo — that would concede the d5-square as a permanent outpost and tear a hole in the centre. Instead defend the e-pawn by developing the bishop to e3, keeping the whole pawn mass intact.
Develop the knight to c3. It supports the centre and readies the answer to the knight jump to b4 — the rook simply steps to c1 and the intruder achieves nothing.
Now the knight comes to f3. With enough pieces out, the pin by the bishop on g4 has lost its sting, so it is time to finish developing and think about castling.

Once Black has castled queenside, the pawn to c5 changes everything: it clamps the position and jump-starts a queenside pawn-storm straight at the black king, with the queen ready to swing out to a4 and join in.
